activity/accelerators-and-brakes|b456c66: If we don't know what we want, it’s hard to communicate our likes and dislikes around sex. This activity is adapted from Emily Nagoski’s ‘Come As You Are’, and can help us understand our bodies and our desire better.
What emotional factors affect how you feel about sex? Does strengthening emotional intimacy increase your desire for sex?
Where do you like to be when you have sex?

These questions can be useful prompts to help us think about what works for us, and what doesn’t. If this activity feels like too much, feel free to pause and take your time. This can be an activity you do at your own pace, in your own time.
This activity is taken from our session ‘
’, in our Healing from sexual trauma course.
For this activity, make a list of your accelerators and brakes.
Accelerators are things that make us want sex and brakes are things that turn us off sex.

This can be an ongoing list that you add to over time, as and when you get in touch with your desire. Not all of our accelerators or brakes will apply to every sexual encounter we have. Things can change, depending on the situation, the context, and who we’re with! If you’re struggling to think of anything, consider the following:
Are there things that you do or don’t like to happen before sex?
Does stress affect your desire for sex? Are there particular kinds of stress that do this?
List what turns your desire on and off, to understand your body and your needs.
activity/ideal-sexual-being|ab941fbd-853: We want to untangle our culture's idea of the 'ideal' sexuality and the ideal of what we want as a sexual being. You can find this activity in the ‘
’ session, from our Healing from sexual trauma course.
This activity, from Emily Nagoski's ‘Come as You Are’ workbook, gives you five questions to answer in two different ways.

Answer these five questions for your culture's Ideal Sexual Being. This is a being that you were raised to believe in. It may help to answer these for your gender so you can dig into specific cultural myths, but do the exercise in whatever way works for you. Here are the five questions:
What does this person look like, and how do they behave outside sexual situations?
How do they initiate sex, if they do?
What do they do, and how do they feel during sex?
How does their partner feel about their sexuality?
What would they never do or experience?
Five questions to unpack your culture's 'ideal' sexuality, and what you truly want.
activity/letter-to-a-part-of-my-body|5dd: This activity explores three different practices for increasing our comfort with our bodies, creating healthy body-image, and taking care of ourselves. This activity is from the ‘
Show your body some love. Cook a nice meal and eat it, have a dance, give yourself a hug, paint your nails, have a bath — whatever feels like an act of care.
’ session, from our Healing from sexual trauma course.

If you feel comfortable, write a letter to a part of your body. It could be on the outside like your shoulders, on the inside like your heart, or even a part that can’t be seen like your voice. There is an example in the bonus content from Session 5 in our Healing from Sexual Trauma course, from a book called 'Written on the Body'—a collection of poems and letters written by trans and non-binary survivors and edited by Lexie Bean.
Some prompts for your letter could be:
Your earliest memory of that body part
Any frustrations or difficulties you’ve had with that body part
How you’ve used that body part
What you are grateful for, and want to thank that part for
Immerse yourself in some diverse body-positive media. It can be hard to imagine things that we can’t see.
Write a caring letter to a part of your body, as a step towards acceptance.
Letter to a part of my body
activity/mapping-fear-and-stress-in-our-: This exercise is about trying to identify where in our bodies we feel stress and fear. You can write it out, draw it, or use one of our templates below. We do this activity as a part of our session ‘
’ in our course, Healing from sexual trauma.

We want to consider our reactions to stress or danger. Do we fight, flee, or freeze? Have we always responded this way or have repeated events taught us this? Is this how we've learned to stay safe? Our goal is to understand how and why our body enters the 3F state (flight, flee or freeze).
Locate what it ‘feels’ like when you’re threatened or anxious so you can learn your body's reactions. Understanding these feelings in advance means we can take care of ourselves in the moment.
Draw out how your stress response feels in your body. See the example stick figure below for inspiration.
Consider what triggers this stress response in you. Have you already worked out what makes you stressed? It could be overhearing the neighbours shouting or getting some feedback at work.
If you can’t identify anything yet, that’s fine. We’re slowly opening our minds to knowing ourselves and how we respond to stress – it's okay if this process takes time.
Draw where stress and fear show up in your body, to understand your body's responses.
Mapping fear and stress in our bodies
activity/stream-of-consciousness-journal: This activity is called stream-of-consciousness and it’s a journaling technique that helps us to release our emotions that are weighing on our minds, by writing them down.
Find a time and way that works for you. Some prefer to do this in the mornings, others before bed, and some do it as and when they feel a lot of emotion
’ session, from our Healing from sexual trauma course.
Stream-of-consciousness journalling involves writing freely for a set, short amount of time.
Set a timer. You can start with 5 minutes and work your way up.
Start writing! You don't need to consider details or structure, just let your thoughts run free. No plans or even full sentences are necessary.

You might write about traumatic events that you’ve experienced during this exercise. Take care of yourself, and notice how you’re feeling as you journal. You can stop at any time if things feel like too much. Use our grounding exercises to help you come back to the present moment, as you need.
Remember that you can always go back and read what you wrote after the time is up, to see what you processed or remembered.
Set a timer and write freely, letting your thoughts and feelings flow without judgment.
activity/thought-diaries|4015f421-fff3-4: Thought diaries are a tangible record of all the things we reflect on, learn, and gain in our Bloom courses.
You can write your thought diary somewhere safe online, in a notebook, or even on a post-it, or the back of an envelope.
If I could remember one thing from today, it would be...
A beautiful thing I saw today was…
Thought diaries are an activity we use a lot throughout our courses, so you will find them in different sessions, such as ‘
’ in our Healing from sexual trauma course.
write down one to three stories about yourself that bring you joy.

The idea is to practice self-compassion and equip ourselves with positive memories. This exercise comes from writer Terese Mailhot. We know that our thoughts, bodies, emotions, and behaviours are interconnected. Through writing, we become more aware of the content of our minds and how this links to the feelings in our bodies. It's often scary and overwhelming when we start writing. But as we begin to make sense of our thoughts and stories, we can untangle the relationship between our past and present, to build a more hopeful future.
If you don’t know where to start, that’s ok! Here are some prompts you can use:
Something I am proud of myself for today is…
A short writing practice to note moments of joy and build self-compassion.
activity/timelines|807cba4e-1da5-46b8-b6: This activity is constructing a personal timeline of how we integrate our trauma stories into the overall narratives of our lives.

To begin, take a piece of paper and draw a horizontal line on it. As a reference point, place an ‘X’ somewhere in the timeline to represent where you are in your life right now. And then, on the left side, put down all those important milestones that have happened so far. Some events you might include are:
the birth of a sibling or a child
meeting an important person, like a best friend
changing jobs, starting a course, or another type of life change
Draw a timeline of your life's milestones to see your story as a whole.
activity/trust-mapping|ba954811-a608-4d4: This is a practical exercise that allows us to think about who we trust in our lives — and how trust is dynamic, and can change as we and our relationships with others change.
You can find this exercise in the session ‘
’, in our Society, patriarchy and sexual trauma course.
In your thought diary, draw two overlapping circles (also known as a ‘Venn Diagram').
Label one circle ‘People I trust now’, and label the other ‘People I trusted when I was growing up’.
Now start filling these circles up. Anyone who falls in both categories, you can put in the middle, where the circles overlap.
Notice, without self-judgment or blame, who goes into which part of the diagram. It's ok if there is no one in the ‘Who I trust now’ category. It can take time to feel able to trust again.
A simple diagram to notice who you trust now, and how that's changed over time.
grounding/grouding-sound-of-claps|8b3bef: Clap and rub your hands together.
Hear the noise and feel the sensation in your hands and arms.
Now stamp your feet and focus on the sound that makes and how your legs feel.
Clap, rub your hands and stamp your feet to feel grounded.
grounding/grounding-affirming-ourselves|: Firm pressure can help us feel calmer. For this exercise, let’s hug ourselves with love.
Now we are going say an affirming thought out loud, like, 'I am in control,' or 'I am safe in this moment.'
Squeeze your shoulders with your hands as you say it one more time.
One more time, squeeze your shoulders and say your affirmation.
Now release. Gently rub your arms as you let go. And relax.
A firm self-hug paired with affirming words of safety.
grounding/grounding-best-check-in|90b09f: A practice derived from Mindfulness Based Symptom Management, the BEST check-in is a way to bring our awareness to various aspects of ourselves. This can be done as a daily practice, multiple times a day, or even in response to feeling distressed or uncomfortable in any way.
Take a moment now to check-in with yourself. Keep your feet planted on the ground, your eyes closed or your gaze on a point in front of you.

Begin by noticing your breath. Observe the micro-movements and sensations that are caused by the breath. Notice the quality of your breath, whether it feels fast-paced or slow, rhythmic or irregular. See if there is anything you can do to make yourself just 5-10% more comfortable.
Shift your attention now to your emotions. Notice what emotions or feelings are present for you right now. Simply observe them, like one would observe the rains from a safe, warm room.

Gradually shift your attention to any sensations that you notice in the body. These could be external sensations like the temperature or breeze on your skin, or internal sensations like ease or tension in various parts of the body. See if there is anything you can do to make yourself just 5-10% more comfortable.
Finally, shift your attention to your thoughts. Once again, simply observe the thoughts as one would observe passing clouds while lying on soft, freshly cut grass.
Having checked in with your breath, emotions, sensations and thoughts; you may gently open your eyes and carry this state of presence and awareness of yourself into the rest of your day.
Check in with your breath, emotions, sensations and thoughts.
grounding/grounding-box-breathing|92616a: Before you get started, make sure that you’re seated upright in a comfortable chair with your feet flat on the floor. Try to be in a stress-free, quiet environment where you can focus on your breathing. We will be doing 4 deep reverse breaths.
Keeping your hands relaxed in your lap with your palms facing up, focus on your posture. You should be sitting up straight. This will help you take deep breaths.
Relax. Slowly get back to your normal breathing and whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes.
Sitting upright, slowly exhale through your mouth, getting all the oxygen out of your lungs. Focus on this intention and be conscious of what you’re doing.
Inhale slowly and deeply through your nose to the count of four. In this step, count to four very slowly in your head.
Feel the air fill your lungs, one section at a time, until your lungs are completely full and the air moves into your abdomen.
Hold your breath for another slow count of four.
Exhale through your mouth for the same slow count of four 1, 2, 3, 4
Hold your breath for the same slow count of four before repeating this process.
A steady four-count breath to ease stress and calm your body.
grounding/grounding-calming-colours|da90: If you feel comfortable, close your eyes.
Now think about a calming colour and as you take a deep breath in, imagine the air that is coming into your body is that colour and it’s calming every part of your body inside of you.
Now as you exhale, imagine a strong colour like red or orange coming out along with your stress, anxiety and fears.
Let’s do this two more times.
Inhale calming colours in…exhale, strong colours out.
Inhale welcoming calmness…exhale releasing stress and anxiety.
Now, whenever you’re ready, slowly open your eyes.
Breathe in calm, breathe out stress, using colour and breath.
grounding/grounding-coming-back-to-your-: We’re going to imagine a place we’ve seen that makes us feel safe.

It can be somewhere you’ve been before, maybe from a holiday or it could be somewhere you’ve heard about in a story. Or it could be somewhere you make up for yourself. Now let’s take three deep breaths together.
Notice the feelings and sensations that come up in your body. Notice if you are feeling positive emotions.
Have another look around and take a mental picture of this place. Save this image.
This is your safe space that you can come back to, whenever you want to feel calm and secure.
Picture a place that feels safe, and hold onto that image.
Coming back to your safe space
grounding/grounding-compassionate-body-s: The goal of this practice is to offer ourselves compassion and build our internal awareness of the body.

Begin by finding a comfortable posture and take a moment to arrive into this practice. You can be seated or lying down, and choose to have your eyes closed or gaze fixed at a point in front of you. We are going to scan the body, part-by-part and bring compassion to each part. If you feel overwhelmed by a feeling associated with a particular area, you can bypass this part of your body and return to it when you are ready.
When you are ready, stretch, wiggle fingers and toes, rotate wrists and ankles, and open your eyes. See if you can carry an attitude of self-compassion into your next activity.

Bring your attention to the forehead, eyes, and jaw, allowing any tension to soften. Rest here for a few moments. If you notice pain or emotional discomfort, bring kind and loving attention to that part of your body.
Move into the neck and throat, allowing them to soften, bringing soothing attention to any tightness or discomfort.

Continue down into the shoulders and chest, filling your body with kindness. Notice any discomfort and invite it to soften. Bring a gentle and kind attention to any pain or emotion. Don’t fight or resist, let it be as it is.

Bring attention to both of your arms simultaneously, from the upper arms down to the fingertips. If this is a difficult time for you, let your hand rest on your heart, feeling this soothing and comforting touch.

Continue with the belly, back, and pelvis, bringing kind, compassionate attention to every part of your body. If difficult feelings arise, either return to your breath or try repeating some of these phrases: May I be safe. May I be healthy. May I be peaceful. May I live with ease. Let these words land, receive them. Let them nourish you.
If you come up against a strong dislike of any part of the body, try saying in the kindest tone you can: May I love and accept my body just as it is. May I bring kindness and compassion to this body.
Bring kind attention to the thighs, knees, ankles, and feet, appreciating all that your body does and how hard it works for you. If you get distracted, return to the phrases or the breath.
End with compassion for your entire body, with all its scars, imperfections, discomforts, or illnesses. See if you can appreciate this body, loving it as it is right now.
A gentle body scan, offering each part kindness.
grounding/grounding-day-walkthrough|42a1: In your head or on a piece of paper, walk through your whole day until the present moment.
You can think about how I woke up, got out of bed, brushed my teeth, made breakfast, looked for my metro card in my room, etc.
Show gratitude to yourself for showing up for yourself through these acts and doing all the things to make you reach this moment.
Retrace your day's small steps and notice how far you've come.
grounding/grounding-drifting-clouds-medi: Visualize yourself in a field lying in the soft grass, breathing in the richness of the earth.
Become aware of your mind and begin to notice the clouds of worry filled thoughts
And these clouds are casting shadows across the landscape of your mind.
Just sit back and watch the clouds of worries pass by. Choose not to go into their expansion, just let it all drift by.

And as all the worry clouds now gradually disband and move out beyond the horizon of your mind you become aware of the quiet spaces in between your thoughts, simply aware of the blue sky. You get a sense of complete freedom.
Time to rest and recuperate from the wear and tear of your thinking.
Time to lie there in the sunshine on the soft grass, feel the sun's rays on you feel the warmth of the sun on your chest and stomach

and let the warmth pour into your mind and as the feeling of well-being rises, all is well within your world, realising the importance of the quality of your thoughts you prioritize to look after your mind.
Let worrying thoughts drift by like clouds, freeing space for calm.
grounding/grounding-finger-focus|c1a1362: This is a somatic practice. You can think of it like a moving meditation. The objective of this practice is to slow down, come into the present moment and stimulate all the nerve-endings in the fingertips. Sit comfortably and gently close your eyes, or let your gaze rest at a point in front of you.
Bring your awareness in your right hand, noticing any sensations that come alive in the right palm when you place your attention on it.
Release the fingers and bring the left thumb to middle finger.
Release.
Thumb to ring finger.
Release.
Thumb to little finger and release.
Now attempt to place your awareness equally across both hands, and bring both thumbs to touch each other.
Release.
Both forefingers come to touch each other and release.
Both middle fingers.
Release.
Slowly bring the right thumb and forefinger to touch.
Both ring fingers.
Release.

Both little fingers and release, relaxing the hands down on your lap and noticing how the palms and fingers feel after this gentle stimulation of the nerve endings. Notice whether the body feels more present and more relaxed than before.
Open your eyes and carry this state of presence and awareness into the rest of your day.
Release the fingers and bring the right thumb and middle finger to touch.
Release.
Right thumb to ring finger.
Release.
Thumb to little finger and release.
Now guide your awareness out of the right hand and shift it into the left, noticing what happens when your left hand suddenly comes into your awareness. We will do the same practice on the left side.
Slowly bring the left thumb and forefinger to touch.
A gentle hand movement to bring you into the present.
Finger focus
grounding/grounding-listen-to-your-voice: Let’s use our voice to help bring us back to the present.
You can say your name or a friend’s name; you can pick up a book and read aloud the first paragraph you see, or just read out the ingredients on a bag of chips!
Whatever it is, make it something that calms you or brings you joy.
Use your voice — say or read something calming — to return to now.
grounding/grounding-positive-coping-stat: Prepare a coping statement for when you begin to feel the onset of anxiety or overwhelm.
My name is Francesca. Everything that is happening now will pass. There will come a time when I can look back on this time without fear or anxiety.
Repeat the above statement or something similar, lingering on each word, and recognize the temporary nature of painful memories and difficult events.
An affirming statement to repeat when anxiety rises.
grounding/grounding-slow-breathing|d0364: We’ll take 3 deep and slow breaths. Find a comfortable spot for yourself. You can sit or lie down. Take your time.
Once you’ve found a comfortable spot, you can close your eyes and start to feel the sensations in your body. We will slowly breathe in to the count of 4.
Count to 4 in your mind and hold.
Now exhale for longer. Count to 8 in your mind and hold.
You can now get your breath to a normal pace. if you’re lying down, curl to the left side of your body and come in a seated position.
Now very slowly, open your eyes. Welcome the new calmness in your body.
Three slow, deep breaths to calm your body and mind.
grounding/grounding-touching-and-feeling: Find any object near to you. It can be smooth or rough or soft. Anything with texture works, even your own carpet!
Focus on what this item feels like in your hands.
How would you describe it? You can even talk out loud about what you are thinking or doing. Using our senses, whether it’s sight, touch, or sound, can remind us of where we are and what’s real.
Use touch and texture nearby to reconnect with your senses.
grounding/grounding-visual-breathing|a08: As the flower expands, take a deep breath in. When the flower folds back in on itself, let the breath out.
Do this six times and see how the breaths feel in your body.
Follow a flower's rhythm in and out to slow your breath.
grounding/grounding-what-can-you-hear|07: Stop and take a moment to listen.
What do you hear? Birds chirping? Cars outside?
Maybe its really quiet where you are and all you can really hear is the sound of your own breath and your heart beating.
Notice and name what sounds you can hear in your body. Start with the closest and loudest sound.
Gradually move your awareness to the sounds outward. So you are focusing on what you can hear at a distance.
Tune into sounds near and far to anchor yourself in the moment.
